cards.explanation: The answer is a very large assembly of Israelites. Ezra the priest is facedown before the house of God, and a very large assembly gathers around him. The text says men, women and children (Ezra 10:1). One man on the ground praying, and then a crowd shows up. I think that's a lot of people to find around you when you lift your head.

The answer is True. Ezra is praying and confessing, weeping and facedown, and the text says the people wept bitterly as well (Ezra 10:1). The crowd isn't standing around watching, friends. They're crying right along with him.

The answer is hope. Shecaniah son of Jehiel, an Elamite, says it right after admitting the unfaithfulness: “…yet in spite of this, there is hope for Israel.” (Ezra 10:2). He says the hard part out loud and still says there's hope. That's a man who looks at a burnt batch and says the oven still works.

The answer is to send away the foreign wives and their children. Shecaniah says, “So now let us make a covenant before our God to send away all the foreign wives and their children…” (Ezra 10:3). He adds, “Let it be done according to the Law.” I think this is a heavy moment, because real families are in it. It's a serious covenant, made before God.

The answer is that the people will support him. Shecaniah says to Ezra, “Get up, for this matter is your responsibility, and we will support you. Be strong and take action!” (Ezra 10:4). Ezra is handed the job and told he won't carry it alone. That's a good thing to hear when the load is this heavy.

The answer is swear. Ezra gets up and makes the leading priests, Levites and all Israel take an oath to do what had been said, and they took the oath (Ezra 10:5). An oath is a serious promise made before God, not a casual nod.

The answer is False. While Ezra stays in the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib, he eats no food and drinks no water (Ezra 10:6). The text says he's mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles. No food, no water, just mourning.

The answer is three. Whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property and be expelled from the assembly of the exiles (Ezra 10:8). That's a short window to get to Jerusalem, friends. I'd have been packing the minute the announcement ended.

The answer is that he loses his property and is expelled from the assembly. Whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property, and would himself be expelled from the assembly of the exiles (Ezra 10:8). The text says this was according to the counsel of the leaders and elders. That's a serious deadline.

The answer is the heavy rain. On the twentieth day of the ninth month, the people sit in the square at the house of God, trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain (Ezra 10:9). So they're trembling over the matter and the heavy rain at the same time. I think that's a rough combination.

The answer is separate. Ezra the priest says, “Now, therefore, make a confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers, and do His will. Separate yourselves from the people of the land and from your foreign wives.” (Ezra 10:11). Confession comes first, then doing God's will. I think this is a heavy thing to say to a crowd, and he says it plainly.

The answer is many people and the rainy season. The assembly answers, “But there are many people here, and it is the rainy season. We are not able to stay out in the open.” (Ezra 10:13). They also say it isn't the work of one or two days. So they agree with Ezra, they just need a plan that works for the weather and the crowd.

The answer is that leaders represent everyone while towns come at set times. The assembly says, “Let our leaders represent the whole assembly. Then let everyone in our towns who has married a foreign woman come at an appointed time…” (Ezra 10:14). So the crowd doesn't have to stand out in the rain, friends. It's a way to handle a big job without everyone being there at once.

The answer is judges. The men come at an appointed time, “…together with the elders and judges of each town…” (Ezra 10:14). So each town sends its own elders and judges along with the men concerned. That's a town-by-town setup.

The answer is the fierce anger of their God. The plan goes on “…until the fierce anger of our God in this matter is turned away from us.” (Ezra 10:14). They say it themselves, and they say it as a group. I think that's a sober thing to hear from a crowd sitting in the rain.

The answer is family heads. Ezra the priest selects men who were family heads, each of them identified by name, to represent their families (Ezra 10:16). So the men chosen are leaders in their own households. It's a good way to get a big job done.

The answer is False. The text says that by the first day of the first month they had dealt with all the men who had married foreign women (Ezra 10:17). They began on the first day of the tenth month (Ezra 10:16). So they went through every case, friends, not half.
